142 VERE (Sir Francis), The COMMENTARIES of, being diverse pieces of service, wherein he had command, written by himself in way of Commentary. Published by WILLIAM DILLINGHAM, D.D., first edition, with fine portraits of Sir Francis and Sir Horace Vere, Lord Nore of Tilbury, and Sir John Ogle [by FAITHORNE] (brilliant impression), a double plate of monument by R. Gaywood, and 6 plates and maps by Vaughan, folio, Large Paper; contemporary mottled calf gilt, with Harleian gold-tooling on sides (FINE COPY), £6.6s

Sir Francis Vere was one of the 'Fighting Veres' (Sir Horace being the other), whose lives were portrayed by Sir Clements Markham. He greatly distinguished himself when serving with the British troops in the Low Countries from 1585 to 1602, an account of which is given in 'his straightforward and soldierlike Commentaries' (D.N.B.). A new edition, with a new title, was published in 1672, and the work was reprinted in Arber's English Garner.

143 VERSTEGAN [alias ROWLANDS] (Richard): A RESTITUTION OF DECAYED INTELLIGENCE in ANTIQUITIES, concerning the most noble and renowned ENGLISH NATION, by the Studie and Trauaille of R. V., first edition, with vignette of the Tower of Babel on title, fine engravings, and the author's engraved arms at end, sm. 4to. contemporary English calf gilt (neally rebacked), with morocco labels (title dust-stained and mounted), £2.10s

Antwerp, Robert Bruney, 1605

This edition is deservedly reckoned the best, as well on account of containing one or more engravings afterwards omitted, as also for the superiority of the plates, those in the subsequent editions being very indifferent copies.—Lowndes.

In this work, which is dedicated to James I., Verstegan protests his English birth. He gives a summary of the early invasions of Great Britain, the formation of its languages, surnames, and other matters, and exhibits his knowledge of Anglo-Saxon.—D.N.B.
The edition is held to be the best, as it contains an index, and also Chronicon ex Chronicus.

145 WILLIAM I.: EUDEMARE (François d', Chanoine de Rouen) HISTOIRE excellente et heroïque du Roy WILLIAUME le BASTARD, jadis Roy d'Angleterre & Duc de Normandie, 12mo. (pp. xii + 615), original limp vellum (margin of title and some ll. slightly water-stained), £1.5s

Originally issued in 1626. 'Ouvrage devenu rare. Il en a des exemplaires avec un nouveau titre au nom de Rob. Feron, et sous la date de 1629 [supra]; mais c'est toujours la même édition, dont on a retranché le f. d'errata.-Brunet. This exhaustive life of William the Conqueror is very little known, and this is probably the reason why it has been neglected by his biographers. The author is not noticed in the biographical dictionaries.

This publication, occasioned by a work of William Petyt, entitled 'Ancient Rights of the Commons of England' (1680), was answered by Dr. Brady in his Introduction to Old English History. It is by some attributed to Atwood, and by others to Cooke or Johnson. —Lowndes. An old MS. note in the above copy attributes it to William Atwood, Chief Justice of New York.

147 WILLIAM of NEWBURGH: HISTORIA ANGLICANA, sive de Regno et Administratione Regum Angliae. In Lucem edita per GUILIELMUM NEUBRIGENSIS [sic] Anglicum. Nunc primum Auctori XI Capitulis hactenus desideratis & Notis JoANNIS PICARDI, sm. 8vo. old parchment, 15s

Parisiiis, 1632

Both in substance and in form it is the finest historical work left to us by an Englishman of the twelfth century.—Miss Kate Norgate. 'His account of the disputes between Henry II. and Beket is singularly free from prejudice. His characters are drawn with much fidelity and discrimination, and he has preserved many interesting anecdotes relating to distinguished persons.'—J. B. Mullinger.
